title: Introspective Coupling: Self-Explanation Training Tracks Behavioral Change Despite Fixed Supervision
claim: A model trained on fixed explanations of its earlier behavior produces explanations matching its own shifted behavior, not its training targets.
layout: 4 colored columns A–D, left-to-right, with curved arrows and match/mismatch markers
description: The figure has four pastel-shaded columns labeled A Base Model, B Training, C Trained Model and D Evaluation. A left margin shows example prompts: a cue-included input with 'Hint: A', a cue-ablated input, and a meta-level question about how the answer would change without the hint. Column A shows the base model M0 with behavior boxes (A and B) and a green ground-truth explanation box, 'Changes from A to B'. Column B uses yellow highlights to say the model is trained on explanations of the original model. Column C shows the trained model Mreg, whose behavior changes. Red struck-out text and 'Changes after training!' mark the shifts. Column D shows the predicted explanation, 'No change from B'. A blue dotted arrow with a green check connects it to the Self explanation (Match). An orange dotted arrow with a red cross connects it to the Orig explanation (No Match). Orange, blue and green boxes carry the colors.
caption: Method overview. (A) We sample behaviors B(M0) from the base model M0 on inputs x, x\C and construct explanation labels E(M0). (B) We fine-tune M0 on these explanations, yielding Mreg. (C) During training, Mreg’s behavior drifts to distribution B(Mreg), so its corresponding explanations shift to E(Mreg). (D) Mreg’s output explanations track this change: they better match explanations of Mreg’s own behavior (Self) despite training on explanations of M0 (Orig). We call this Self > Orig introspective coupling.
abstract: When does training language models (LMs) to generate explanations of their predictions yield faithful introspection, rather than superficial imitation? We study LMs trained to explain which features of their inputs influenced their behavior, using models' counterfactual behavior on modified inputs as supervision. Surprisingly, we find that LMs trained on fixed counterfactual explanations derived from their earlier checkpoints, or even from behaviorally similar models in different families, frequently produce explanations more faithful to their own current behaviors than to those of their training targets. This "introspective" coupling between LM explanations and behaviors occurs when training explanations remain sufficiently correlated with current behaviors over the course of training, even as behaviors themselves shift. We also show that introspective coupling tracks behavior shifts: when explanation training is provided concurrently with other post-training objectives, explanations change to match without requiring updated supervision. This phenomenon appears in multiple tasks, including sycophancy and refusal, and is robust to label noise. Overall, our results show that even fixed datasets of counterfactual explanations can provide scalable and generalizable post-training signal for introspection.
